Prime-to-p\displaystyle p étale covers of algebraic groups and homogeneous spaces

Michel Brion and Tamás Szamuely Address: Université de Grenoble I, Département de Mathématiques, Institut Fourier, UMR 5582 du CNRS, 38402 Saint-Martin d’Hères Cedex, France Email address: Michel.Brion@ujf-grenoble.fr Address: Alfréd Rényi Institute of Mathematics, Hungarian Academy of Sciences, Reáltanoda utca 13-15, H-1053 Budapest, Hungary Email address: szamuely.tamas@renyi.mta.hu
Date: August 24, 2026

1. Introduction

By a classical result of Schreier [24], the fundamental group of a connected and locally connected topological group G\displaystyle G is commutative. If moreover G\displaystyle G is (semi-)locally simply connected, then every Galois cover ϕ:Y→G\displaystyle\phi:\,Y\to G carries a group structure for which ϕ\displaystyle\phi is a homomorphism. Thus G\displaystyle G is the quotient of Y\displaystyle Y by an abelian normal subgroup.

The first part of the following proposition states an analogue of this result in algebraic geometry. The second part gives a bound on the number of topological generators of the prime-to-p\displaystyle p fundamental group. To state it, we need to introduce some notation. Recall that by Chevalley’s theorem G\displaystyle G is an extension of an abelian variety A\displaystyle A by a linear algebraic group Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm aff} (see [4], [5], [6], [22]). Denote by g\displaystyle g the dimension of A\displaystyle A and by r\displaystyle r the rank of Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm aff} (which is by definition the dimension of a maximal torus). Furthermore, denote by 𝐙(p′)\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})} the direct product of the rings 𝐙ℓ\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{\ell} for ℓ≠p\displaystyle\ell\neq p.

Proposition 1.1.

Let G\displaystyle G be a connected algebraic group over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p≥0\displaystyle p\geq 0.

  1. a)

    Every étale Galois cover Y→G\displaystyle Y\to G of degree prime to p\displaystyle p carries the structure of a central isogeny. In particular, the maximal prime-to-p\displaystyle p quotient π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G) of the étale fundamental group of G\displaystyle G is commutative.

  2. b)

    The group π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G) is a quotient of 𝐙(p′)2​g+r\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}^{2g+r}.

By convention, all Galois covers are assumed to be connected. Statement OPENa)\displaystyle a) was known in the special cases where G\displaystyle G is an abelian variety (Lang–Serre [12]) or G\displaystyle G is affine (Miyanishi [16], Magid [14]). Note that restricting to prime-to-p\displaystyle p covers is crucial because if one allows p\displaystyle p-covers in characteristic p>0\displaystyle p>0, the statement fails disastrously already for the additive group 𝐆a\displaystyle{\bf G}_{a} (Raynaud [21]).

In part OPENb)\displaystyle b) the bound is sharp (take the direct product of an abelian variety and a torus). In the case when G\displaystyle G is commutative it follows from Theorem 1.1 and ([26], §6.4, Cor. 4) that π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G) is moreover a free 𝐙(p′)\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}-module. However, in the non-commutative case it may contain torsion. For instance, π1​(SO​(n))\displaystyle\pi_{1}({\rm SO}(n)) in characteristic 0 is of order 2. (Of course, in this case the bound on the number of generators given by the proposition is very far from the truth.)

We also prove a generalization to homogeneous spaces. Bounding the topological rank is more difficult than in the group case, so we state this result as a theorem.

Theorem 1.2.

Keep the assumptions of the proposition above, and let X\displaystyle X be a variety on which G\displaystyle G acts transitively with connected stabilizers.

  1. a)

    Every étale Galois cover of X\displaystyle X of degree prime to p\displaystyle p is of the form G~/H~\displaystyle\tilde{G}/\tilde{H} for a central isogeny G~→G\displaystyle\tilde{G}\to G and a lift H~\displaystyle\tilde{H} of the stabilizer H\displaystyle H of a point of X\displaystyle X in G~\displaystyle\tilde{G}.

  2. b)

    The group π1(p′)​(X)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(X) is a quotient of 𝐙(p′)2​(g−gH)+r−rH\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}^{2(g-g_{H})+r-r_{H}}, where gH\displaystyle g_{H} and rH\displaystyle r_{H} are the dimension of the abelian variety quotient and the rank of the subgroup H\displaystyle H, respectively.

In work in progress, M. Borovoi and C. Demarche [2] have obtained an extension of statement OPENa)\displaystyle a) to non-connected H\displaystyle H. In this case H~\displaystyle\tilde{H} is a finite index subgroup of the preimage of H\displaystyle H in G~\displaystyle\tilde{G}. However, statement OPENb)\displaystyle b) fails when the isotropy group H\displaystyle H is not connected. For example, if Γ\displaystyle\Gamma is a finite group of order prime to p\displaystyle p and Γ↪GL⁡(n)\displaystyle\Gamma\hookrightarrow{\rm GL}(n) a faithful representation, then π1(p′)​(GL⁡(n)/Γ)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}({\rm GL}(n)/\Gamma) is just Γ\displaystyle\Gamma.

We also present an application of Proposition 1.1 which was our original motivation for studying the problem. It concerns commutative algebraic groups.

Theorem 1.3.

Let G\displaystyle G be a connected commutative algebraic group over an algebraically closed field k\displaystyle k. For n\displaystyle n prime to the characteristic there is an exact sequence

0→Pic​G/n​Pic​G→Hom⁡(Λ2​(Gn),μn)→Brn​G→00\to{\rm{Pic\,}}G/n\/{\rm{Pic\,}}G\to{\rm{Hom}}(\Lambda^{2}({}_{n}G),\mu_{n})\to{}_{n}{\rm{Br\,}}G\to 0

where Pic​G\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}G and Br​G\displaystyle{\rm{Br\,}}G denote the Picard and Brauer groups of G\displaystyle G, respectively, and Gn\displaystyle{}_{n}G stands for the n\displaystyle n-torsion part of G\displaystyle G.

The case where G\displaystyle G is an abelian variety was established by Berkovich [1]. The proof in the general case uses Proposition 1.1 as an input, in the identification of the group Hom⁡(Gn,μn)\displaystyle{\rm{Hom}}({}_{n}G,\mu_{n}) with the étale cohomology group H1​(G,μn)\displaystyle H^{1}(G,\mu_{n}). However, this identification can also be derived using a more elementary method; see the conclusion of Section 4.

The following almost immediate corollary of Theorem 1.3 makes a classical formula of Grothendieck ([9], corollaire 3.4) explicit in the case of a connected commutative algebraic group G\displaystyle G.

Corollary 1.4.

Let ℓ\displaystyle\ell be a prime number different from the characteristic of k\displaystyle k. The ℓ\displaystyle\ell-primary torsion part of Br​G\displaystyle{\rm{Br\,}}G is isomorphic to (𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ)(2​g+r)​(2​g+r−1)/2−ρ\displaystyle({\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell})^{(2g+r)(2g+r-1)/2-\rho}, where g\displaystyle g and r\displaystyle r are defined as above, and ρ\displaystyle\rho is the rank of the Néron–Severi group of A\displaystyle A, the abelian variety quotient of G\displaystyle G.

Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.4 will be proven in Section 4.

We thank Mikhail Borovoi, Antoine Chambert-Loir, Cyril Demarche, Hélène Esnault, Ofer Gabber and Jakob Stix for very helpful remarks. The second author was partially supported by OTKA grant No. NK81203.

2. Algebraic groups

In this section we prove Proposition 1.1. Our first proof of statement OPENa)\displaystyle a) was quite involved, using, among other ingredients, a fairly recent result of Orgogozo [20] on compatibility of the prime-to-p\displaystyle p fundamental groups with products. As Hélène Esnault pointed out, this result together with a modification of the classical argument of Lang and Serre for abelian varieties suffices for the proof of the statement. We briefly recall the argument (see the original paper [12] or [27], Theorem 5.6.10 and Remark 5.6.11 for more details).

Denote by mG:G×G→G\displaystyle m_{G}:\,G\times G\to G the group operation of G\displaystyle G. Given an étale Galois cover Y→G\displaystyle Y\to G of degree prime to p\displaystyle p, consider the fibre product square

Y′=(G×G)×GY→Y↓↓ϕG×G→mGG.\begin{CD}Y^{\prime}=(G\times G)\times_{G}Y@>{}>{}>Y\\ @V{}V{}V@V{}V{\phi}V\\ G\times G@>{m_{G}}>{}>G.\end{CD}

One checks that Y′\displaystyle Y^{\prime} is also connected, hence Y′→G×G\displaystyle Y^{\prime}\to G\times G is a Galois étale cover with group Γ:=Aut⁡(Y|G)\displaystyle\Gamma:={\rm Aut}(Y|G). Since the prime-to-p\displaystyle p fundamental group is compatible with direct products (Orgogozo [20], Cor. 4.9), there exist étale Galois covers Z1→G\displaystyle Z_{1}\to G and Z2→G\displaystyle Z_{2}\to G, with groups Γ1\displaystyle\Gamma_{1} and Γ2\displaystyle\Gamma_{2}, respectively, such that Y′\displaystyle Y^{\prime} is a quotient of the direct product Z1×Z2→G×G\displaystyle Z_{1}\times Z_{2}\to G\times G. In particular, there is a normal subgroup Δ⊂Γ1×Γ2\displaystyle\Delta\subset\Gamma_{1}\times\Gamma_{2} with Γ≅(Γ1×Γ2)/Δ\displaystyle\Gamma\cong(\Gamma_{1}\times\Gamma_{2})/\Delta. Replacing the Zi\displaystyle Z_{i} by their quotients by the actions of the Γi∩Δ\displaystyle\Gamma_{i}\cap\Delta we may assume Δ∩Γi={1}\displaystyle\Delta\cap\Gamma_{i}=\{1\} for i=1,2\displaystyle i=1,2. Thus the Γi\displaystyle\Gamma_{i} may be identified with normal subgroups of Γ\displaystyle\Gamma that generate Γ\displaystyle\Gamma and centralize each other. But by construction the base change Y2′→{1}×G\displaystyle Y_{2}^{\prime}\to\{1\}\times G of Y′\displaystyle Y^{\prime} by the map {1}×G→G×G\displaystyle\{1\}\times G\to G\times G must be an étale Galois cover with group Γ2\displaystyle\Gamma_{2}, and similarly for the base change Y1′→G×{1}\displaystyle Y_{1}^{\prime}\to G\times\{1\}. It follows that Γ=Γ1=Γ2\displaystyle\Gamma=\Gamma_{1}=\Gamma_{2}, and Γ\displaystyle\Gamma is commutative. Moreover, we have isomorphisms Zi≅Yi′≅Y\displaystyle Z_{i}\cong Y_{i}^{\prime}\cong Y for i=1,2\displaystyle i=1,2. This yields a map Y×Y→Y′\displaystyle Y\times Y\to Y^{\prime}, whence also a map mY:Y×Y→Y\displaystyle m_{Y}:\,Y\times Y\to Y by composing with the projection Y′→Y\displaystyle Y^{\prime}\to Y. Fix a point 1Y\displaystyle 1_{Y} of Y\displaystyle Y in the fibre above the neutral element of G\displaystyle G. Modifying mY\displaystyle m_{Y} by an automorphism of Y\displaystyle Y if necessary we may assume mY​(1Y,1Y)=1Y\displaystyle m_{Y}(1_{Y},1_{Y})=1_{Y}. A standard argument ([27], pp. 180–181) then shows that mY\displaystyle m_{Y} equips Y\displaystyle Y with the structure of an algebraic group.

We now turn to the proof of part OPENb)\displaystyle b) and take up the notation introduced before the statement of the proposition. We already know that π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G) is commutative. In the case when G\displaystyle G is an abelian variety of dimension g\displaystyle g it is moreover free over 𝐙(p′)\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})} of rank 2​g\displaystyle 2g (see e.g. [27], Theorem 5.6.10 and Remark 5.6.11). Hence it will be enough to prove the following: the natural map α∗:π1(p′)​(G)→π1(p′)​(A)\displaystyle\alpha_{*}:\,\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)\to\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(A) induced by the projection α:G→A\displaystyle\alpha:\,G\to A is surjective and its kernel is a quotient of 𝐙(p′)r\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}^{r}.

Denote by 𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′)\displaystyle{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})} the direct sum of the torsion abelian groups 𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ\displaystyle{\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell} for ℓ≠p\displaystyle\ell\neq p. Since π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G) is commutative, there is a perfect pairing

π1(p′)​(G)×Hét1​(G,𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))→𝐐/𝐙\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)\times H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{1}(G,{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})})\to{\bf Q}/{\bf Z}

obtained by passing to the limit from the perfect pairings

π1(p′)​(G)/m​π1(p′)​(G)×Hét1​(G,𝐙/m​𝐙)→𝐙/m​𝐙\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)/m\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)\times H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{1}(G,{\bf Z}/m{\bf Z})\to{\bf Z}/m{\bf Z}

for m\displaystyle m prime to p\displaystyle p.

The Leray spectral sequence

Hétp​(A,𝐑q​α∗​𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))⇒Hétp+q​(G,𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{p}(A,{\bf R}^{q}\alpha_{*}{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})})\Rightarrow H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{p+q}(G,{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})})

associated with the projection α\displaystyle\alpha yields an exact sequence

0→Hét1​(A,α∗​𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))\displaystyle\displaystyle 0\to H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{1}(A,\alpha_{*}{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}) →Hét1​(G,𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))→\displaystyle\displaystyle\to H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{1}(G,{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})})\to
→Hét0​(A,𝐑1​α∗​𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′)).\displaystyle\displaystyle\to H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{0}(A,{\bf R}^{1}\alpha_{*}{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}).

As α\displaystyle\alpha has connected fibres, Hét1​(A,α∗​𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))≅Hét1​(A,𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))\displaystyle H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{1}(A,\alpha_{*}{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})})\cong H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{1}(A,{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}), which shows that the map between the first two terms in the above exact sequence is the 𝐐/𝐙\displaystyle{\bf Q}/{\bf Z}-dual of the map α∗:π1(p′)​(G)→π1(p′)​(A)\displaystyle\alpha_{*}:\,\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)\to\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(A). It follows that the latter map is surjective.

The stalk of the étale sheaf 𝐑1​α∗​𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′)\displaystyle{\bf R}^{1}\alpha_{*}{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})} at a geometric point can be identified with Hét1​(Gaff,𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))\displaystyle H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{1}(G_{\rm aff},{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}). Pick a maximal torus T⊂Gaff\displaystyle T\subset G_{\rm aff}. Miyanishi proves in ([16], Lemma 3) that the natural map π1(p′)​(T)→π1(p′)​(Gaff)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(T)\to\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G_{\rm aff}) is surjective (see also Lemma 3.4 below for a more general statement). Since π1(p′)​(T)≅π1(p′)​(𝐆m)r≅𝐙(p′)r\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(T)\cong\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}({\bf G}_{m})^{r}\cong{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}^{r}, this bounds the number of generators of π1(p′)​(Gaff)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G_{\rm aff}) by r\displaystyle r. But since α\displaystyle\alpha is smooth, the sheaf 𝐑1​α∗​𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′)\displaystyle{\bf R}^{1}\alpha_{*}{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})} is locally constant and thus Hét0​(A,𝐑1​α∗​𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))\displaystyle H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{0}(A,{\bf R}^{1}\alpha_{*}{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}) becomes a subgroup of Hét1​(T,𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))≅(𝐐(p′)/𝐙(p′))r\displaystyle H_{\mbox{\scriptsize\'{e}t}}^{1}(T,{\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})})\cong({\bf Q}_{(p^{\prime})}/{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})})^{r}. By taking 𝐐/𝐙\displaystyle{\bf Q}/{\bf Z}-duals we obtain that the kernel of α∗:π1(p′)​(G)→π1(p′)​(A)\displaystyle\alpha_{*}:\,\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)\to\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(A) is indeed a quotient of 𝐙(p′)r\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}^{r}.

Remarks 2.1.

1. In the course of the above proof we have in fact constructed a homotopy exact sequence

π1(p′)​(Gaff)→π1(p′)​(G)→π1(p′)​(A)→0.\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G_{\rm aff})\to\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)\to\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(A)\to 0.

The paper [2] contains a generalization of this exact sequence to homogeneous spaces which is constructed using our Theorem 1.2 OPENa)\displaystyle a). Note that a general homotopy exact sequence of prime-to-p\displaystyle p fundamental groups for morphisms with non-proper fibres is not known at present.

2. Jakob Stix has shown us the following very quick argument for the commutativity of π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G). The point is that by a well-known reasoning π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G) is a group object in the category of groups. In more detail: by compatibility of the functor π1(p′)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})} with products ([20], Cor. 4.9 again) the multiplication map of G\displaystyle G induces a map m:π1(p′)​(G)×π1(p′)​(G)→π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle m:\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)\,\times\,\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G)\to\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G) that satisfies the group axioms by functoriality, and moreover m⁡(1,g)=m⁡(g,1)=g\displaystyle m(1,g)=m(g,1)=g for all g∈π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle g\in\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G). The calculation

h​g=m⁡(1,h)​m​(g,1)=m⁡((1,h)​(g,1))=m⁡(g,h)hg=m(1,h)m(g,1)=m((1,h)(g,1))=m(g,h)
=m⁡((g,1)​(1,h))=m⁡(g,1)​m​(1,h)=g​h=m((g,1)(1,h))=m(g,1)m(1,h)=gh

shows that this group law is commutative and coincides with the usual group law of π1(p′)​(G)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{(p^{\prime})}(G).

3. Homogeneous spaces

In this section we prove Theorem 1.2. We begin the proof of part OPENa)\displaystyle a) with some standard observations and reductions. Let X\displaystyle X be a variety on which a connected algebraic group G\displaystyle G acts transitively. Choose a point x∈X\displaystyle x\in X and denote by H⊂G\displaystyle H\subset G its isotropy subgroup scheme. Then X≅G/H\displaystyle X\cong G/H and the natural map G/Hred→G/H\displaystyle G/H_{\rm red}\to G/H is finite, surjective and purely inseparable, where Hred\displaystyle H_{\rm red} denotes the reduced part of H\displaystyle H. It follows that the induced map π1​(G/Hred)→π1​(G/H)\displaystyle\pi_{1}(G/H_{\rm red})\to\pi_{1}(G/H) is an isomorphism. So we may assume throughout that H\displaystyle H is is an algebraic group; moreover, as in the statement of the theorem, we assume it is connected.

Assume now f:X~→X\displaystyle f:\tilde{X}\to X is an étale Galois cover with group Γ\displaystyle\Gamma of order prime to p\displaystyle p. Consider the orbit map φ:G→X\displaystyle\varphi:G\to X, g↦g⋅x\displaystyle g\mapsto g\cdot x, and form the cartesian square

G~→φ~X~π↓f↓G→φX.\begin{CD}\tilde{G}@>{\tilde{\varphi}}>{}>\tilde{X}\\ @V{\pi}V{}V@V{f}V{}V\\ G@>{\varphi}>{}>X.\\ \end{CD}

Since φ\displaystyle\varphi is a flat (hence open) surjection with connected fibres, so is φ~\displaystyle\tilde{\varphi}, so we infer from the connectedness of X~\displaystyle\tilde{X} that G~\displaystyle\tilde{G} is connected as well. By Proposition 1.1 OPENa)\displaystyle a) the map π\displaystyle\pi is therefore a central isogeny with kernel Γ\displaystyle\Gamma. The algebraic subgroup π−1​(H)⊂G~\displaystyle\pi^{-1}(H)\subset\tilde{G} is a disjoint union of fibres of φ~\displaystyle\tilde{\varphi}; denote by H~\displaystyle\tilde{H} its neutral component. Since H\displaystyle H is connected by assumption, the map π|H~:H~→H\displaystyle\pi|_{\tilde{H}}:\,\tilde{H}\to H must be an isomorphism. Moreover, the map φ~\displaystyle\tilde{\varphi} is invariant under H~\displaystyle\tilde{H} since so is f​φ~=φ​π\displaystyle f\tilde{\varphi}=\varphi\pi\/ and f\displaystyle f is finite étale (see e.g. [27], Corollary 5.3.3). Thus φ~\displaystyle\tilde{\varphi} factors through a morphism G~/H~→X~\displaystyle\tilde{G}/\tilde{H}\to\tilde{X}, which is an isomorphism since so is the morphism G/H→X\displaystyle G/H\to X. This completes the proof of statement OPENa)\displaystyle a).

We now turn to the rank estimate of part OPENb)\displaystyle b). Given X=G/H\displaystyle X=G/H as in the statement, we may assume without harm that G\displaystyle G acts faithfully on X\displaystyle X. Indeed, the (scheme-theoretic) kernel K\displaystyle K of the action is contained in H\displaystyle H. Then G/K\displaystyle G/K acts faithfully on X\displaystyle X with connected stabilizer H/K\displaystyle H/K. By the lemma on p. 154 of [15] (see also [4], Corollary 2.1.9) the quotient H/K\displaystyle H/K is affine. Thus the dimension gH\displaystyle g_{H} of the maximal abelian quotient of H\displaystyle H equals that of the reduced neutral component of K\displaystyle K, and hence the dimension of the maximal abelian quotient of G/K\displaystyle G/K is g−gH\displaystyle g-g_{H}. Thus we may replace G\displaystyle G by G/K\displaystyle G/K and H\displaystyle H by H/K\displaystyle H/K and have a natural map αX:X=G/H→G/Gaff=A\displaystyle\alpha_{X}:X=G/H\to G/G_{\rm aff}=A (which is in fact the Albanese morphism of X\displaystyle X, but we shall not need this).

Case I: the base field k\displaystyle k has characteristic 0\displaystyle 0. The fundamental group of X\displaystyle X being topologically finitely generated ([10], Exp. II), it does not change by extensions of algebraically closed fields by the argument of ([27], p. 186; see also [20], Theorem 4.11). Thus we reduce to the case k=𝐂\displaystyle k={\bf C} where the algebraic fundamental group is the profinite completion of the topological fundamental group π1top​(X)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(X) ([8], Exp. XII, Cor. 5.2). It is then enough to see that π1top​(X)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(X) is a quotient of 𝐙2​g+r−rH\displaystyle{\bf Z}^{2g+r-r_{H}}. The fibration αX\displaystyle\alpha_{X} with fibre Gaff/H\displaystyle G_{\rm aff}/H yields an exact sequence

π1top​(Gaff/H)→π1top​(X)→π1top​(A)≅𝐙2​g.\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(G_{\rm aff}/H)\to\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(X)\to\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(A)\cong{\bf Z}^{2g}.

Thus it remains to show that π1top​(Gaff/H)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(G_{\rm aff}/H) is a quotient of 𝐙r−rH\displaystyle{\bf Z}^{r-r_{H}}.

Choose a maximal torus TH⊂H\displaystyle T_{H}\subset H and then a maximal torus T⊂Gaff\displaystyle T\subset G_{\rm aff} containing TH\displaystyle T_{H}. Then we have a commutative diagram

T→Gaff↓↓T/TH→Gaff/H\begin{CD}T@>{}>{}>G_{\rm aff}\\ @V{}V{}V@V{}V{}V\\ T/T_{H}@>{}>{}>G_{\rm aff}/H\\ \end{CD}

and hence a similar commutative diagram of induced homomorphisms of topological fundamental groups.

Let B\displaystyle B be a Borel subgroup of Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm aff} containing T\displaystyle T. The flag variety Gaff/B\displaystyle G_{\rm aff}/B is simply connected, and therefore the natural map π1top​(B)→π1top​(Gaff)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(B)\to\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(G_{\rm aff}) is surjective. Also, B=T×U\displaystyle B=T\times U as a variety, where U⊂B\displaystyle U\subset B denotes the unipotent part. Since U\displaystyle U is isomorphic to an affine space, the natural map π1top​(T)→π1top​(B)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(T)\to\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(B) is surjective as well, whence the surjectivity of the composite map π1top​(T)→π1top​(Gaff)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(T)\to\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(G_{\rm aff}) (note that Miyanishi’s argument mentioned in the previous section is an algebraic variant of this reasoning).

As Gaff→Gaff/H\displaystyle G_{\rm aff}\to G_{\rm aff}/H is a quotient map with connected fibres, the map π1top​(Gaff)→π1top​(Gaff/H)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(G_{\rm aff})\to\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(G_{\rm aff}/H) is also surjective, hence so is the map π1top​(T/TH)→π1top​(Gaff/H)\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(T/T_{H})\to\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(G_{\rm aff}/H). But T/TH\displaystyle T/T_{H} is a torus of rank r−rH\displaystyle r-r_{H}, therefore π1top​(T/TH)≅𝐙r−rH\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm top}(T/T_{H})\cong{\bf Z}^{r-r_{H}}, which completes the proof of the characteristic 0 case.

Case II: k\displaystyle k has characteristic p>0\displaystyle p>0. The argument will be a variant of the above but will use more background from the structure theory of algebraic groups.

Recall from ([7], III.3.8 and [22], Corollary 5, p. 440) that

G=Gaff​Gant,G=G_{\rm aff}G_{\rm ant},

where Gant⊂G\displaystyle G_{\rm ant}\subset G denotes the largest anti-affine subgroup (that is, the largest subgroup with 𝒪⁡(Gant)=k\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(G_{\rm ant})=k); moreover, Gant\displaystyle G_{\rm ant} is connected and central in G\displaystyle G. In positive characteristic Gant\displaystyle G_{\rm ant} is in fact a semi-abelian variety ([3], Proposition 2.2).

As before, choose a maximal torus TH⊂H\displaystyle T_{H}\subset H and then a maximal torus T⊂Gaff\displaystyle T\subset G_{\rm aff} containing TH\displaystyle T_{H}. Concerning T​Gant\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant} we shall prove below the following key proposition.

Proposition 3.1.

The natural map

π1​(T​Gant)(p′)→π1​(G)(p′)\pi_{1}(TG_{\rm ant})^{(p^{\prime})}\to\pi_{1}(G)^{(p^{\prime})}

is surjective.

Assuming the proposition, consider the commutative diagram

T​Gant→G↓↓(T​Gant)/TH→G/H.\begin{CD}TG_{\rm ant}@>{}>{}>G\\ @V{}V{}V@V{}V{}V\\ (TG_{\rm ant})/T_{H}@>{}>{}>G/H.\\ \end{CD}

The right vertical map induces a surjection on fundamental groups because the pullback of any connected étale cover of G/H\displaystyle G/H to G\displaystyle G remains connected, as in the proof of statement OPENa)\displaystyle a). Proposition 3.1 and the induced diagram on prime-to-p\displaystyle p fundamental groups then imply the surjectivity of the map

π1​((T​Gant)/TH)(p′)→π1​(G/H)(p′).\pi_{1}((TG_{\rm ant})/T_{H})^{(p^{\prime})}\to\pi_{1}(G/H)^{(p^{\prime})}.

Observe now that T​Gant\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant} is a semi-abelian variety which is an extension of an abelian variety of dimension g\displaystyle g by a torus of rank r\displaystyle r. To prove this fact, remark first that T\displaystyle T contains the maximal torus of the semi-abelian variety Gant\displaystyle G_{\rm ant}, since that torus is central in Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm aff}. Thus T​Gant\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant} is also a semi-abelian variety, with maximal torus T\displaystyle T and abelian quotient

T​Gant/T≅Gant/(Gant∩T).TG_{\rm ant}/T\cong G_{\rm ant}/(G_{\rm ant}\cap T).

But Gant∩T\displaystyle G_{\rm ant}\cap T is an affine subgroup scheme of Gant\displaystyle G_{\rm ant} containing (Gant)aff\displaystyle(G_{\rm ant})_{\rm aff} (the maximal torus of Gant\displaystyle G_{\rm ant}), hence the quotient (Gant∩T)/(Gant)aff\displaystyle(G_{\rm ant}\cap T)/(G_{\rm ant})_{\rm aff} is finite. Likewise, the quotient (Gant∩Gaff)/(Gant)aff\displaystyle(G_{\rm ant}\cap G_{\rm aff})/(G_{\rm ant})_{\rm aff} is finite. It follows that the abelian quotient of T​Gant\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant} is isogenous to Gant/(Gaff∩Gant)≅G/Gaff=A\displaystyle G_{\rm ant}/(G_{\rm aff}\cap G_{\rm ant})\cong G/G_{\rm aff}=A.

We conclude that (T​Gant)/TH\displaystyle(TG_{\rm ant})/T_{H} is an extension of an abelian variety of dimension g\displaystyle g by a torus of dimension r−rH\displaystyle r-r_{H}, and hence its prime-to-p\displaystyle p fundamental group is a quotient of 𝐙(p′)2​g+r−rH\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{(p^{\prime})}^{2g+r-r_{H}} by the results of the previous section. This finishes the proof of case II modulo Proposition 3.1.

The proof of Proposition 3.1 will require a series of lemmas.

Lemma 3.2.

If f:X→Y\displaystyle f:X\to Y is a torsor under a connected unipotent group, then the natural map π1​(X)→π1​(Y)\displaystyle\pi_{1}(X)\to\pi_{1}(Y) is surjective.

Proof.

By writing the unipotent group as an iterated extension of copies of 𝐆a\displaystyle{\bf G}_{a} we reduce by induction to the case where f\displaystyle f is a 𝐆a\displaystyle{\bf G}_{a}-torsor. Then f\displaystyle f has a compactification by the projective line bundle f¯:X×𝐆a𝐏1→Y\displaystyle{\bar{f}:X\times^{{\bf G}_{a}}{\bf P}^{1}\to Y}, where 𝐆a\displaystyle{\bf G}_{a} acts on 𝐏1\displaystyle{\bf P}^{1} by translations. The complement of X\displaystyle X in X×𝐆a𝐏1\displaystyle X\times^{{\bf G}_{a}}{\bf P}^{1} is a divisor which yields a section of f¯\displaystyle\bar{f}. So the assertion follows from [8], Exposé XIII, Proposition 4.1 and Example 4.4.        

Returning to our situation, we choose a Borel subgroup B\displaystyle B of G\displaystyle G (or equivalently, of Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm aff}) containing T\displaystyle T. Then B​Gant\displaystyle BG_{\rm ant} is a connected solvable subgroup of G\displaystyle G, since Gant\displaystyle G_{\rm ant} is connected and central in G\displaystyle G.

Lemma 3.3.

The natural map

π1​(B​Gant)(p′)→π1​(G)(p′)\pi_{1}(BG_{\rm ant})^{(p^{\prime})}\to\pi_{1}(G)^{(p^{\prime})}

is surjective.

Proof.

Choose another Borel subgroup B−\displaystyle B^{-} such that the intersection B∩B−\displaystyle B\cap B^{-} is of smallest dimension. Specifically, consider the unipotent radical Ru​(G)=Ru​(Gaff)\displaystyle R_{u}(G)=R_{u}(G_{\rm aff}). Then Gaff/Ru​(G)\displaystyle G_{\rm aff}/R_{u}(G) is a connected reductive group with Borel subgroup B/Ru​(G)\displaystyle B/R_{u}(G), and we take for B−\displaystyle B^{-} the preimage in G\displaystyle G of an opposite Borel subgroup ([11], §26.2). Denoting by U−\displaystyle U^{-} the unipotent part of B−\displaystyle B^{-}, we have B∩U−=Ru​(G)\displaystyle B\cap U^{-}=R_{u}(G) (as schemes), since U−\displaystyle U^{-} contains Ru​(G)\displaystyle R_{u}(G) and the intersection (B/Ru​(G))∩(U−/Ru​(G))\displaystyle(B/R_{u}(G))\cap(U^{-}/R_{u}(G)) is trivial. It follows that

(B​Gant)∩U−=B⁡(Gant∩Gaff)∩U−=B∩U−=Ru​(G),(BG_{\rm ant})\cap U^{-}=B(G_{\rm ant}\cap G_{\rm aff})\cap U^{-}=B\cap U^{-}=R_{u}(G),

where the first equality holds since Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm aff} contains B\displaystyle B and U−\displaystyle U^{-}, and the second one since Gant∩Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm ant}\cap G_{\rm aff} is contained in the center of Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm aff} and hence in the Borel subgroup B\displaystyle B. Now the multiplication in G\displaystyle G yields a map

f:B​Gant×U−→Gf:BG_{\rm ant}\times U^{-}\to G

making B​Gant×U−\displaystyle BG_{\rm ant}\times U^{-} a torsor under (B​Gant)∩U−=Ru​(G)\displaystyle(BG_{\rm ant})\cap U^{-}=R_{u}(G). The image of f\displaystyle f is open in G=Gaff​Gant\displaystyle G=G_{\rm aff}G_{\rm ant}, since B​U−=B​B−\displaystyle BU^{-}=BB^{-} is open in Gaff\displaystyle G_{\rm aff}. Thus the pullback of any connected étale cover of G\displaystyle G to the image B​Gant​U−\displaystyle BG_{\rm ant}U^{-} is connected, and hence the natural map

π1​(B​Gant​U−)→π1​(G)\pi_{1}(BG_{\rm ant}U^{-})\to\pi_{1}(G)

is surjective. But by Lemma 3.2 the map

π1​(B​Gant×U−)→π1​(B​Gant​U−)\pi_{1}(BG_{\rm ant}\times U^{-})\to\pi_{1}(BG_{\rm ant}U^{-})

is surjective as well. This implies the surjectivity of the natural map

π1​(B​Gant×U−)(p′)→π1​(G)(p′)\pi_{1}(BG_{\rm ant}\times U^{-})^{(p^{\prime})}\to\pi_{1}(G)^{(p^{\prime})}

and in turn the lemma, by using ([20], Cor. 4.9) again, and recalling that the variety U−\displaystyle U^{-} is an affine space.        

Lemma 3.4.

The natural map

π1​(T​Gant)(p′)→π1​(B​Gant)(p′)\pi_{1}(TG_{\rm ant})^{(p^{\prime})}\to\pi_{1}(BG_{\rm ant})^{(p^{\prime})}

is surjective.

Proof.

First note that B=U​T\displaystyle B=UT, and hence B​Gant=U​T​Gant\displaystyle BG_{\rm ant}=UTG_{\rm ant}. This yields a torsor U×T​Gant→B​Gant\displaystyle U\times TG_{\rm ant}\to BG_{\rm ant} under the group scheme U∩T​Gant\displaystyle U\cap TG_{\rm ant}. The latter is commutative, finite (since its reduced neutral component is unipotent and diagonalizable), and unipotent, hence of order a power of p\displaystyle p. Write G1\displaystyle G_{1} for the quotient of U×T​Gant\displaystyle U\times TG_{\rm ant} by the reduced part of U∩Gant\displaystyle U\cap G_{\rm ant}. The natural map G1→B​Gant\displaystyle G_{1}\to BG_{\rm ant} is finite, surjective and purely inseparable, therefore it induces an isomorphism on fundamental groups ([8], exposé IX, théorème 4.10). We may thus assume G1=B​Gant\displaystyle G_{1}=BG_{\rm ant}, in which case U×T​Gant→B​Gant\displaystyle U\times TG_{\rm ant}\to BG_{\rm ant} is a finite étale cover with group Γ:=U∩T​Gant\displaystyle\Gamma:=U\cap TG_{\rm ant}. We thus obtain an exact sequence

1→π1​(U×T​Gant)→π1​(B​Gant)→Γ→11\to\pi_{1}(U\times TG_{\rm ant})\to\pi_{1}(BG_{\rm ant})\to\Gamma\to 1

of fundamental groups. But Γ\displaystyle\Gamma is a p\displaystyle p-group, and hence the natural map π1​(U×T​Gant)(p′)→π1​(B​Gant)(p′)\displaystyle\pi_{1}(U\times TG_{\rm ant})^{(p^{\prime})}\to\pi_{1}(BG_{\rm ant})^{(p^{\prime})} is an isomorphism. We now conclude as in the proof of the previous lemma.        

Combining the two lemmas above we obtain the surjectivity of the natural map

π1​(T​Gant)(p′)→π1​(G)(p′),\pi_{1}(TG_{\rm ant})^{(p^{\prime})}\to\pi_{1}(G)^{(p^{\prime})},

as stated in Proposition 3.1.

Remark 3.5.

In the course of the above proof we have in fact shown that in characteristic p>0\displaystyle p>0 the subgroup T​Gant⊂G\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant}\subset G is a semi-abelian variety which is an extension by T\displaystyle T of an abelian variety isogenous to A\displaystyle A. If p=0\displaystyle p=0 the same holds for the image of T​Gant\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant} in G/Ru​(G)\displaystyle G/R_{u}(G). A similar argument shows that (in all characteristics) the subgroup B​Gant\displaystyle BG_{\rm ant} is an extension by B\displaystyle B of an abelian variety isogenous to A\displaystyle A.

One shows easily that B​Gant\displaystyle BG_{\rm ant} is a maximal connected solvable subgroup of G\displaystyle G and moreover all such subgroups are conjugate in G\displaystyle G. Likewise, T​Gant\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant} (resp. the image of T​Gant\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant} in G/Ru​(G)\displaystyle G/R_{u}(G)) is a maximal semi-abelian variety if p>0\displaystyle p>0 (resp. p=0\displaystyle p=0), and all such subgroups are conjugate. Thus B​Gant\displaystyle BG_{\rm ant} is a subgroup of G\displaystyle G that is analogous to a Borel subgroup in the linear case, and T​Gant\displaystyle TG_{\rm ant} is analogous to a maximal torus.

4. Application to Brauer groups

In this section we prove Theorem 1.3. We need two lemmas, in which all cohomology groups are taken with respect to the étale topology.

Lemma 4.1.

Let G\displaystyle G be a connected commutative algebraic group over an algebraically closed field k\displaystyle k. For n\displaystyle n prime to the characteristic the cohomology ring H∗​(G,𝐙/n​𝐙)\displaystyle H^{*}(G,{\bf Z}/n{\bf Z}) with its cup-product structure is canonically isomorphic to the exterior algebra Λ∗​H1​(G,𝐙/n​𝐙)\displaystyle\Lambda^{*}H^{1}(G,{\bf Z}/n{\bf Z}).

Proof.

The group G\displaystyle G is an extension of a semi-abelian variety G1\displaystyle G_{1} by a connected commutative unipotent group U\displaystyle U. Since U\displaystyle U is an iterated extension of 𝐆a\displaystyle{\bf G}_{a}’s, we may view G\displaystyle G as an affine bundle over G1\displaystyle G_{1}. But then the cohomology of G\displaystyle G with finite coefficients identifies with that of G1\displaystyle G_{1}. So we may assume that G\displaystyle G is a semi-abelian variety, extension of an abelian variety A\displaystyle A by a torus T\displaystyle T. In this case the proof is a direct generalization of the argument for abelian varieties as in [18] Theorem 15.1. Here is a brief sketch. By formal cohomological arguments as in loc. cit. one sees that it is enough to prove the lemma with 𝐐ℓ\displaystyle{\bf Q}_{\ell}-coefficients instead of 𝐙/n​𝐙\displaystyle{\bf Z}/n{\bf Z}-coefficients, where ℓ\displaystyle\ell is a prime invertible in k\displaystyle k. Then one invokes an algebraic lemma ([18], Lemma 15.2) based on Borel’s fundamental structure theorem for Hopf algebras. It shows that it is enough to check that there exists an integer m>0\displaystyle m>0 such that Hi​(G,𝐐ℓ)=0\displaystyle H^{i}(G,{\bf Q}_{\ell})=0 for i>m\displaystyle i>m and moreover H1​(G,𝐐ℓ)\displaystyle H^{1}(G,{\bf Q}_{\ell}) has dimension ≤m\displaystyle\leq m over 𝐐ℓ\displaystyle{\bf Q}_{\ell}. We check these properties for m=2​g+r\displaystyle m=2g+r, where g=dim​A\displaystyle g={\rm{dim\,}}A and r=dim​T\displaystyle r={\rm{dim\,}}T. In the Leray spectral sequence for α:G→A\displaystyle\alpha:\,G\to A

E2p​q=Hp​(A,Rq​α∗​𝐐ℓ)⇒Hp+q​(G,𝐐ℓ)E_{2}^{pq}=H^{p}(A,R^{q}\alpha_{*}{\bf Q}_{\ell})\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(G,{\bf Q}_{\ell})

the terms E2p​q\displaystyle E_{2}^{pq} vanish for p>2​g\displaystyle p>2g (because A\displaystyle A has cohomological dimension 2​g\displaystyle 2g) and q>r\displaystyle q>r (because T\displaystyle T has cohomological dimension r\displaystyle r, being affine of dimension r\displaystyle r). This shows the first property. For the second property, observe first that there is an isomorphism Gn≅(𝐙/n​𝐙)2​g+r\displaystyle{}_{n}G\cong({\bf Z}/n{\bf Z})^{2g+r} because the sequence

0→Tn→Gn→An→00\to{}_{n}T\to{}_{n}G\to{}_{n}A\to 0

is split exact by n\displaystyle n-divisibility of T\displaystyle T; moreover, there are isomorphisms Tn≅(𝐙/n​𝐙)r\displaystyle{}_{n}T\cong({\bf Z}/n{\bf Z})^{r} and An≅(𝐙/n​𝐙)2​g\displaystyle{}_{n}A\cong({\bf Z}/n{\bf Z})^{2g}. Thus it suffices to apply the next lemma.        

Lemma 4.2.

Under the assumptions of Lemma 4.1 the map

Hom⁡(Gn,μn)→H1​(G,μn){\rm{Hom}}({}_{n}G,\mu_{n})\to H^{1}(G,\mu_{n})

sending a character χ:Gn→μn\displaystyle\chi:\,{}_{n}G\to\mu_{n} to the class of the μn\displaystyle\mu_{n}-torsor over G\displaystyle G obtained by pushing out the extension

(1) 0→Gn→G→G→00\to\,{}_{n}G\to G\to G\to 0

by χ\displaystyle\chi is an isomorphism.

Proof.

To prove injectivity, assume that a pushout of (1) by a nontrivial character gives a split torsor over G\displaystyle G. By construction it is then a split extension of G\displaystyle G by a cyclic group of order dividing n\displaystyle n which is also a quotient of G\displaystyle G. This is impossible because G\displaystyle G is n\displaystyle n-divisible.

For surjectivity assume given a μn\displaystyle\mu_{n}-torsor π:Y→G\displaystyle\pi:\,Y\to G. Assume first Y\displaystyle Y is connected. By Proposition 1.1 OPENa)\displaystyle a) there is an algebraic group structure on Y\displaystyle Y making it a central extension of G\displaystyle G; in particular it is commutative. (Indeed, since μn⊂Y\displaystyle\mu_{n}\subset Y is central and G\displaystyle G is commutative, the commutator map Y×Y→Y,(y,z)↦y​z​y−1​z−1\displaystyle Y\times Y\to Y,\,(y,z)\mapsto yzy^{-1}z^{-1} induces a map G×G→μn\displaystyle G\times G\to\mu_{n} which must be constant as G\displaystyle G is connected.) By the same argument as for abelian varieties ([19], Remark p. 169 or [27], Corollary 5.6.9) the multiplication-by-n\displaystyle n map G→G\displaystyle G\to G factors through π\displaystyle\pi, which gives in particular a character χ:Gn→μn\displaystyle\chi:\,{}_{n}G\to\mu_{n} by looking at the fibres above the neutral element. There is thus a map of μn\displaystyle\mu_{n}-torsors from the pushforward of (1) by χ\displaystyle\chi to Y\displaystyle Y which must be an isomorphism. If Y\displaystyle Y is not connected, it is induced from a connected μm\displaystyle\mu_{m}-torsor for some m|n\displaystyle m|n which in turn comes from a character Gm→μm\displaystyle{}_{m}G\to\mu_{m}. The character corresponding to Y\displaystyle Y is obtained by extending this character to Gn\displaystyle{}_{n}G in a way compatible with the induction of torsors.        

Remark 4.3.

It follows from the above proof that the extension (1) gives the largest abelian étale Galois cover of G\displaystyle G of exponent n\displaystyle n. Indeed, an easy argument using the Leray spectral sequence as in the proof of Lemma 4.1 shows that H1​(G,μn)\displaystyle H^{1}(G,\mu_{n}) is finite. As before, after choosing an isomorphism μn≅𝐙/n​𝐙\displaystyle\mu_{n}\cong{\bf Z}/n{\bf Z} we may identify connected μn\displaystyle\mu_{n}-torsors and étale 𝐙/n​𝐙\displaystyle{\bf Z}/n{\bf Z}-Galois covers. So we infer that there is a largest finite étale Galois cover whose Galois group is abelian of exponent n\displaystyle n, and this Galois group is isomorphic to H1​(G,μn)\displaystyle H^{1}(G,\mu_{n}). By the above proof it must be a quotient of the étale cover given by (1), but then the quotient map is an isomorphism by maximality.

Proof of Theorem 1.3. The Kummer sequence in étale cohomology coming from the exact sequence

1→μn→𝐆m→𝐆m→11\to\mu_{n}\to{\bf G}_{m}\to{\bf G}_{m}\to 1

of étale sheaves yields an exact sequence

0→Pic​G/n​Pic​G→H2​(G,μn)→Brn​G→00\to{\rm{Pic\,}}G/n{\rm{Pic\,}}G\to H^{2}(G,\mu_{n})\to{}_{n}{\rm{Br\,}}G\to 0

which we may rewrite using Lemma 4.1 as

0→Pic​G/n​Pic​G→Λ2​H1​(G,μn)⊗μn⊗−1→Brn​G→0.0\to{\rm{Pic\,}}G/n{\rm{Pic\,}}G\to\Lambda^{2}H^{1}(G,\mu_{n})\otimes\mu_{n}^{\otimes-1}\to{}_{n}{\rm{Br\,}}G\to 0.

We may then replace H1​(G,μn)\displaystyle H^{1}(G,\mu_{n}) by Hom⁡(Gn,μn)\displaystyle{\rm{Hom}}({}_{n}G,\mu_{n}) using Lemma 4.2.        

Proof of Corollary 1.4. Setting n=ℓm\displaystyle n=\ell^{m} in the exact sequence of Theorem 1.3 and passing to the direct limit over m\displaystyle m we obtain an exact sequence

0→Pic​G⊗𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ→Hom⁡(Λ2​Tℓ​(G),𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ)→Br​G​{ℓ}→00\to{\rm{Pic\,}}G\otimes{\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell}\to{\rm{Hom}}(\Lambda^{2}T_{\ell}(G),{\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell})\to{\rm{Br\,}}G\{\ell\}\to 0

where Tℓ​(G)\displaystyle T_{\ell}(G) is the ℓ\displaystyle\ell-adic Tate module of G\displaystyle G and Br​G​{ℓ}\displaystyle{\rm{Br\,}}G\{\ell\} denotes the ℓ\displaystyle\ell-primary torsion of Br​G\displaystyle{\rm{Br\,}}G. As the Hom-group in the middle is ℓ\displaystyle\ell-divisible, so is Br​G​{ℓ}\displaystyle{\rm{Br\,}}G\{\ell\}, hence it is isomorphic to a finite direct power of 𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ\displaystyle{\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell}. To determine this power explicitly, we calculate the left and middle terms.

For the left term, we use first that Pic​G\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}G is isomorphic to Pic​G/U\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}G/U as in the proof of Lemma 4.1, where U\displaystyle U denotes the largest connected unipotent subgroup of G\displaystyle G. So we may assume that G\displaystyle G is an extension of A\displaystyle A by the torus T=𝐆mr\displaystyle T={\bf G}_{m}^{r}. Now recall that by virtue of a generalization of the Barsotti–Weil formula ([25], VII, §3) the extension G\displaystyle G of A\displaystyle A by T\displaystyle T is classified by a homomorphism c:X∗​(T)→A∗\displaystyle c:\,X^{*}(T)\to A^{*}, where A∗=Pic0​A\displaystyle A^{*}={\rm{Pic\,}}^{0}A is the dual abelian variety and X∗​(T)\displaystyle X^{*}(T) the character group of T\displaystyle T. It fits into an exact sequence

(2) X∗​(T)→cPic​A→α∗Pic​G→0{\rm X}^{*}(T)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle c}}{{\to}}{\rm{Pic\,}}A\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\alpha^{*}}}{{\to}}{\rm{Pic\,}}G\to 0

whose exactness follows, for instance, from ([13], Theorem 5).

Thus Pic​G\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}G is the quotient of Pic​A\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}A by a subgroup of A∗\displaystyle A^{*}. Since A∗\displaystyle A^{*} is ℓ\displaystyle\ell-divisible, we get that Pic​G\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}G is an extension of NS​A\displaystyle{\rm{NS\,}}A by an ℓ\displaystyle\ell-divisible group, whence an isomorphism Pic​G⊗𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ≅NS​A⊗𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}G\otimes{\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell}\cong{\rm{NS\,}}A\otimes{\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell}. Moreover, we have NS​A≅𝐙ρ\displaystyle{\rm{NS\,}}A\cong{\bf Z}^{\rho} by definition of ρ\displaystyle\rho. Finally, the group Hom⁡(Λ2​Tℓ​(G),𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ)\displaystyle{\rm{Hom}}(\Lambda^{2}T_{\ell}(G),{\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell}) is isomorphic to (𝐐ℓ/𝐙ℓ)(2​g+r)​(2​g+r−1)/2\displaystyle({\bf Q}_{\ell}/{\bf Z}_{\ell})^{(2g+r)(2g+r-1)/2}. This follows from the fact that the 𝐙ℓ\displaystyle{\bf Z}_{\ell}-rank of Tℓ​(G)\displaystyle T_{\ell}(G) is 2​g+r\displaystyle 2g+r, as calculated at the end of the proof of Lemma 4.1.        

In conclusion, we remark that in the above proof (more precisely, in Lemma 4.2) we used Proposition 1.1 in a crucial way, which in turn was based on the difficult noncommutative result of Orgogozo [20]. However, for the proof of Lemma 4.2 it is sufficient to know that μn\displaystyle\mu_{n}-torsors over commutative algebraic groups carry a commutative group scheme structure. This fact can be proven in a much more elementary way, as we now explain.

We reduce as above to the case where G\displaystyle G is a semi-abelian variety. A μn\displaystyle\mu_{n}-torsor G~\displaystyle\tilde{G} over G\displaystyle G comes from a line bundle L\displaystyle L of order n\displaystyle n on G\displaystyle G together with a trivialization of L⊗n\displaystyle L^{\otimes n} (see e.g. [17], p. 125). It thus corresponds to a class of order n\displaystyle n in Pic​G\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}G which, by exact sequence (2), comes from a class in Pic​A\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}A. As the Néron–Severi group of A\displaystyle A is torsion free, the latter must be a class in Pic0​A\displaystyle{\rm{Pic\,}}^{0}A, and therefore it is represented by a line bundle whose associated 𝐆m\displaystyle{\bf G}_{m}-torsor Y\displaystyle Y carries a group scheme structure making it a central extension of A\displaystyle A by 𝐆m\displaystyle{\bf G}_{m}. The 𝐆m\displaystyle{\bf G}_{m}-torsor L∗\displaystyle L^{*} associated with L\displaystyle L is the pullback of Y\displaystyle Y to G\displaystyle G, so it comes from a central extension of G\displaystyle G by 𝐆m\displaystyle{\bf G}_{m}. Since 𝒪(L∗)≅⊕n=−∞∞H0(G,L⊗n)\displaystyle\mathcal{O}(L^{*})\cong\oplus_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}H^{0}(G,L^{\otimes n}), the trivialization of L⊗n\displaystyle L^{\otimes n} can be identified with a regular invertible function ψ\displaystyle\psi on L∗\displaystyle L^{*}, and then G~\displaystyle\tilde{G} is the zero subscheme of the regular function ψ−1\displaystyle\psi-1 on G\displaystyle G. When choosing the group structure on L∗\displaystyle L^{*} we may assume that ψ\displaystyle\psi takes the neutral element of L∗\displaystyle L^{*} to 1. But then by Rosenlicht’s lemma ([23], Theorem 3) ψ\displaystyle\psi is a character of the group L∗\displaystyle L^{*}, hence G~⊂L∗\displaystyle\tilde{G}\subset L^{*} is a subgroup scheme. This defines a commutative group scheme structure on G~\displaystyle\widetilde{G} making it a central extension of G\displaystyle G by μn\displaystyle\mu_{n}.
